newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenian PM quits, president names successor.
newsitem.headline: Armenian PM quits, president names successor.

text.p: Armenian Prime Minister Grant Bagratyan resigned on Monday, in a move clearly aimed at soothing tension caused by President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's controversial re-election six weeks ago.
The presidential press service said Ter-Petrosyan had already signed a decree naming Armen Sarkisyan, currently Armenia's ambassador to Britain, to replace Bagratyan, 38.
The 43-year-old physicist who will be Ter-Petrosyan's fifth prime minister in five years in the office.
Bagratyan did not say whether Ter-Petrosyan had asked him to quit. "This involves myself and the president. It was my decision," he told a news conference.
Some observers said that while Bagratyan's departure might help heal wounds left after the divisive election, they expected other major changes in Ter-Petrosyan's government.
Ter-Petrosyan sent tanks into the streets of the capital Yerevan and arrested dozens of political opponents after demonstrators accusing him of vote-rigging turned violent.

The Central Elections Commission said he took 51.8 percent to 41.3 percent for another former prime minister, Vazgen Manukyan. But the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said major violations marred voting.
Ter-Petrosyan just cleared a 50 percent hurdle needed to avoid a second round runoff with Manukyan, who is in hiding, fearing arrest.

Bagratyan called for dialogue between the government and its foes. "We need to be above personal ambitions and political leaders must understand that it is forbidden to use power granted by the state for personal ends," he said.

Bagratyan stewarded three and a half years of wrenching economic reforms after the breakup of the Soviet Union, in a period in which the rocky country fought a war with neighboring Azerbaijan over territory and suffered crippling power shortages.

He became a lightning rod for opposition groups who said that reforms had been too drastic and benefited too few people, but was credited by organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank with taking bold steps needed to start to get the economy back on track.
After a near complete collapse, Armenia's economy has been growing gradually for months and inflation is under control.
"We have managed to pull the country out of the abyss. Time will judge our work," he said.

But Bagratyan said he agreed with opposition charges that the country's wealth had been too unevenly distributed during the reform process. "Capital is concentrated in the hands of a small group of people."
